title: Distributed Inner-Product Estimation for Continuous-Variable Quantum States
authors: Jun Tang; Congcong Zheng; Xutao Yu; Zaichen Zhang
problem: Two separate platforms may each prepare a complex multimode bosonic state with no tractable classical description, yet they cannot measure jointly. How can they compare the states, by estimating \(\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\sigma)\), with only local measurements and classical communication? Discrete-variable protocols do not carry over, because the state space is infinite-dimensional.
result: A protocol using only homodyne detection at shared random phases gives an unbiased estimate of a truncated inner product, with explicit guarantees. Under a mean-energy bound, the number of copies scales as \(\epsilon^{-(2M+2)}\log(2/\delta)\) for \(M\) modes. For Gaussian states, this improves to \(\epsilon^{-2}[\log(2M/\epsilon)]^{2M}\log(2/\delta)\).
significance: Homodyne detection is the standard measurement of continuous-variable optics, so the protocol needs no new hardware and no state reconstruction. The bounds also identify what costs what: the factor \(\epsilon^{-2M}\) comes from truncating phase space, not from statistics, and it is the only part that Gaussian structure improves.
limitations: Copy counts are exponential in the mode number and are sufficient conditions, which the authors call conservative; the sections we read prove no matching lower bound. For instance, a single mode with \(E=1\), \(\epsilon=0.1\) and \(\delta=0.05\) gives about \(10^7\) phase settings by Equation (28). The platforms must share a calibrated phase reference and a quadrature normalisation, and the guarantee assumes a known energy bound. A separate paper on the same topic, 2610.39912, appeared the same day.
summary_basis: Description based on Sections 1–4.1 and Appendix C.1 of the linked arXiv version, read 2026-11-01; Section 4.2 (the Bernstein bound), Section 5 (numerics), and the proofs in Appendices B and C.2 were not read.
methods_basis: Based on the linked paper version. Derivations marked as editorial, and suggested uses in other problems, are editorial guidance rather than results of the paper.
description: Two platforms hold \(M\)-mode states \(\rho,\sigma\). With Weyl operators \(W(\mathbf u)=e^{i\mathbf u^{\mathsf T}\hat{\mathbf R}}\) and characteristic functions \(\chi_\tau(\mathbf u)=\operatorname{Tr}[\tau W(\mathbf u)]\), the Plancherel identity gives \[\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\sigma)=\frac1{(2\pi)^M}\int_{\mathbb R^{2M}}\chi_\rho(\mathbf u)\chi_\sigma(-\mathbf u)\,d\mathbf u.\] This writes the inner product as a phase-space integral of a product of local quantities, which is the opening needed for an LOCC protocol. The question is how to sample this integral with accessible measurements and how much it costs.

A homodyne measurement at a list of phases \(	heta_1,\dots,	heta_M\) gives direct access to a slice: the Fourier transform of its outcomes is \(\chi_\tau\) on the line through the origin at those phases. So if both platforms measure at the same random phases, the expectation of \(e^{i\mathbf s^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf x-\mathbf y)}\) is the integrand at the point \(\mathbf u\) with components \(s_\ell(\cos	heta_\ell,\sin	heta_\ell)\). The integral over all of phase space would have unbounded weights, so the authors truncate to a product of disks of radius \(R\), obtaining \(f_R\) and a bounded estimator.

The error splits into statistical error and truncation bias. Hoeffding's inequality handles the first, since the single-setting statistic is bounded by \(c_R=(R^2/2)^M\), so \(N_\theta\ge8c_R^2\log(2/\delta)/\epsilon^2\) suffices when the bias is at most \(\epsilon/2\). The bias is controlled by assumptions on the states: \((4ME+2M)/R^2\) under a mean-energy bound \(E\) per mode, and \(M\exp[-R^2/2(4ME+2M)]\) for Gaussian states.

Choosing \(R\) to make the bias \(\epsilon/2\) gives the two sufficient setting counts, and the total number of copies is \(2nN_\theta\). A complementary Bernstein bound brings in the dependence on \(n\), the shots per setting. The sections we read do not settle whether the exponential scaling in \(M\) is necessary.

methods.technique: Sampling a phase-space integral through homodyne slices
methods.explanation: The estimator turns a \(2M\)-dimensional integral into random phases measured physically and radial variables integrated analytically, so that no sampling is wasted on the part that can be done by hand.
math: Write each mode's phase-space point in signed polar form, \((u_{q,\ell},u_{p,\ell})=s_\ell(\cos\theta_\ell,\sin\theta_\ell)\). The Jacobian is \(\prod_\ell|s_\ell|\). So drawing \(\theta_\ell\) uniformly on \([0,\pi)\) and \(s_\ell\) with density \(q_R(s)=|s|/R^2\) on \([-R,R]\) makes \(\mathbf u\) uniform on the product of disks.

By the Fourier-slice relation, conditional on the phases the outcomes satisfy \(\mathbb E[e^{i\mathbf s^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf x-\mathbf y)}]=\chi_\rho(\mathbf u)\chi_\sigma(-\mathbf u)\). Averaging over \(\mathbf u\), multiplying by the volume factor \(c_R=(R^2/2)^M\) and keeping the real part gives \(f_R\). So the statistic is unbiased.

The radial average can be done exactly, which can only reduce variance, by the law of total variance. For one mode, \[\psi_R(t)=\frac2{R^2}\int_0^Rs\cos(st)\,ds=\frac{2[Rt\sin(Rt)+\cos(Rt)-1]}{(Rt)^2}.\] So each setting contributes \[W_i=\frac{c_R}{n^2}\sum_{a,b}\prod_\ell\psi_R\big(x^{(a)}_{i,\ell}-y^{(b)}_{i,\ell}\big).\]

Editorial check: for two coherent states of one mode with exact overlap \(0.67032\) and \(R=6\), direct quadrature of \(f_R\) gave \(0.67032\), confirming the normalisation of the Plancherel identity and Jacobian. Simulating the estimator with \(n=1\) and \(2\times10^5\) settings gave \(0.687\pm0.018\), consistent with the target, and every sample respected \(|W|\le c_R=18\). The formula for \(\psi_R\) agreed with numerical integration to seven digits. The estimator's large standard error, with this many settings, shows why these counts are high.
methods.transfer: If a quantity is a phase-space integral of a product of two local functions, shared randomness plus independent slices estimates it without joint measurement. Do by hand any part of the average that needs no data. The method needs a shared phase reference; without one, the slices do not line up.

methods.explanation: Truncation needs a tail bound on \(\chi_\tau\), and the only assumption is finite energy. The argument converts mean energy into a quadratic moment of the characteristic function.
math: Define \(I_\tau=(2\pi)^{-M}\int\|\mathbf u\|^2|\chi_\tau(\mathbf u)|^2d\mathbf u\). Since commuting \(\hat R_j\) with \(W(\mathbf u)\) brings down a component of \(\Omega\mathbf u\), Plancherel gives \(I_\tau=\sum_j\|[\hat R_j,\tau]\|_2^2\).

Each term expands to \(2\operatorname{Tr}(\hat R_j^2\tau^2)-2\operatorname{Tr}(\hat R_j\tau\hat R_j\tau)\), and the second trace is nonnegative. With \(\sum_j\hat R_j^2=2\hat N+M\) and \(\tau^2\preceq\tau\), this gives \[I_\tau\le4\operatorname{Tr}(\tau\hat N)+2M\le4ME+2M.\]

Outside the truncation domain some mode has radius above \(R\), so \(\|\mathbf u\|^2/R^2\ge1\). Inserting this factor and applying Cauchy–Schwarz gives \[|f-f_R|\le\frac{\sqrt{I_\rho I_\sigma}}{R^2}\le\frac{4ME+2M}{R^2}.\] This inverse-square decay is the source of the extra cost: \(R^2\sim1/\epsilon\) makes \(c_R^2\sim\epsilon^{-2M}\). For Gaussian states, with exponential tails, \(R^2\sim\log(1/\epsilon)\).

Editorial check: for two vacuum states the exact bias is \(e^{-R^2/2}\), and it lies below both stated bounds at \(R=1,2,3,5\): for example \(0.0111\) against \(0.222\) and \(0.105\) at \(R=3\). We also recomputed the two copy-count formulas at \(M=1\), \(E=1\), \(\epsilon=0.1\), \(\delta=0.05\): about \(1.06\times10^7\) and \(9.5\times10^5\) settings. The Gaussian advantage is thus modest at this accuracy and grows only as \(\epsilon\) falls.
methods.transfer: For bosonic estimation tasks, a physical energy bound can stand in for compactness: turn it into a moment bound through commutators, then use Markov-style tail control. Expect only algebraic decay from one moment. Stronger tails need stronger assumptions, such as Gaussianity or bounds on higher moments of \(\hat N\).
